title: Building an AI-driven village game where NPCs feel like real people — Devlog #1
author: kkogong07
selftext:
Hey r/aigamedev,

I'm working on a village simulation game where players spend their day talking with AI NPCs and interacting with the world around them.

The long-term goal is fairly ambitious:

* NPCs that feel genuinely human and interesting to talk to
* Quests that emerge dynamically from interactions instead of being hand-authored
* AI-generated assets that blend naturally into the game world

Of those three, the third one is what I'm currently spending most of my time on.

# The problem I'm trying to solve

I think generating a 3D mesh is rapidly becoming the easy part.

Making that asset usable inside an actual game is where things get difficult.

My current pipeline looks like this:

Pixel Art → Image Generation → Trellis.2 → Remesh → UV Unwrap → Game Asset

I intentionally start from pixel art because it helps keep a consistent visual style across generated assets.

The challenge is everything after Trellis.

Once the mesh exists, I still need to solve:

* Poly count optimization
* Remeshing
* UV generation
* Texture quality
* Runtime performance
* Generation latency

And every improvement seems to come with a tradeoff somewhere else.

# UVs are currently my biggest headache

Remeshing is annoying but manageable.

UV unwrapping is where things start to feel more like magic than engineering.

I can get functional UVs.

I can get automated UVs.

But getting clean UV layouts that consistently hold up across arbitrary AI-generated geometry is proving much harder than I expected.

I'm curious how others are approaching this.

For those experimenting with AI-generated 3D assets:

* Are you relying on automatic UV tools?
* Using AI-assisted UV generation?
* Accepting lower-quality UVs and compensating elsewhere?
* Building custom pipelines?

# Why I'm skeptical of fully generative pipelines

One conclusion I've reached so far:

The "generate everything automatically" approach sounds great, but I'm not convinced it's production-ready.

Most end-to-end AI asset pipelines I've tested either:

* take too long,
* produce inconsistent results,
* or require enough cleanup that the automation benefit starts disappearing.

Right now I'm leaning toward hybrid workflows where AI handles generation and deterministic tools handle optimization.

# Small experiment

To explore this problem, I built a small housing sandbox where players can generate 3D objects and place them into a scene:

[https://echo-town.com](https://echo-town.com)

The goal isn't really the housing system itself.

It's a testing ground for evaluating whether generated assets actually feel like they belong in a living game world.

If you try it and notice obvious problems with the asset pipeline, visual consistency, performance, or workflow, I'd genuinely appreciate the feedback.

I'd especially love to hear from anyone who has already fought the UV/remesh battle and come out the other side.

Looking forward to learning from others working on similar AI game development problems.

comments.author: Tyrannicus100BC
comments.body:
We haven’t solved UV unwrapping either. Our artist cuts seams and manually unwraps. We also weight paint by hand (with auto tools for a rough first pass). 

We built a custom web tool to handle prompt -> mesh, built for high concurrency to overcome the long latencies. Our artist is working on dozens of characters / objects at a time, ping pinging between them as AI steps complete. It’s critical to have a nice tool to manage this, otherwise you drown in an ocean of browser tabs.

replies.author: kkogong07
replies.body:
The difference in our case is that UV unwrapping has to happen in a live in-game environment, not during the normal game asset production stage.

As someone who has worked with 3D assets before, I honestly wanted to make the UVs look cleaner because UVs from generative AI assets often look really messy. But if the asset is only going to be used inside the game, I’m starting to wonder if the UVs really need to look nice at all.

Also, if we try to fully automate UV unwrapping, the quality might actually get worse because of the limitations of the algorithm.

replies.author: Tyrannicus100BC
replies.body: We do UV unwrapping because we do a layer of AI texture regeneration for variation on the same mesh. If you’re just going to be displaying the mesh with the original generated texture, what improvement are you hoping to achieve by unwrapping? If it’s all going to be UGC and you’ll never have to touch the asset again as part of any other workflow, who cares if the UVs are messy or neat? It’ll render the same.

replies.author: kkogong07
replies.body:
Actually, we provide 'download' as a GLB file format in [https://echo-town.com/](https://echo-town.com/)  
That was actually the starting point of my concern.

To be honest, we don’t necessarily have to provide a download feature, but some people may want to own the assets, so we offer it as an optional extra feature.

May I ask what algorithm or approach you’re using for UV unwrapping?

replies.author: Tyrannicus100BC
replies.body: Nothing fancy. Mesh cleanup tools in blender, then manual seam marking, then just uv -> unwrap. Art not a science :)

comments.author: alasthennars
comments.body:
Is it too much to ask to NOT use AI at least for your devlog? Do you think a blatantly AI-generated post is genuinely interesting to read? Because I immediately click out as soon as I saw that.

In 5 years time, I'm afraid we will have people unable to communicate without AI, and we'll drown in bulletpoints and redundant subtitles like "why this is important".

replies.author: kkogong07
replies.body:
Thanks for the feedback! That was my mistake.

I’ve been relying on AI quite a lot lately, so when I wrote the post, I was thinking of it as using AI to give my own writing one more pass and make it a bit cleaner.

But I completely understand what you’re saying, and I’ll be more careful starting with my next devlog!  
Even though my English is not very strong, I’ll do my best to express myself in my own words. I hope you’ll understand if it sounds a little awkward.

replies.author: alasthennars
replies.body:
Thank you for taking the criticism constructively. Even if English is not your native language, there is a beauty to using your own words that I think AI will never attain. Stuff you write thanks to actual neurons firing electrical and chemical signals in your brain will *always* feel more genuine than this bulletpoint/subtitle hell that AI loves to feed us.

All the best in your endeavours!

replies.author: kkogong07
replies.body:
I really like your expression, "stuff you write thanks to actual neurons firing electrical and chemical signals".  
I absolutely enjoy the signal processing.

replies.author: kkogong07
replies.body: Haha, fairly ambitious! Because we have a great tool, we should have fairy ambition.

comments.author: alexpopescu801
comments.body: When you talk to your audience, especially now that you're small and unknown, you better write yourself otherwise people will wipe the floor with you because you post AI slop. So if you want your reputation to go up instead of down, get rid of AI slop posting because it infuriates everyone. Also you should consider adding one-two screenshots in your post if you want people to click on a link.

replies.author: kkogong07
replies.body:
Thanks for the feedback.

To be honest, I really did try to write the post myself. I also wanted to share the pipeline we actually tried and get some opinions on the situation we’re currently facing.

But I was worried that my writing might not communicate things clearly enough, so I used AI to retouch it one more time, and I think that led to some unfortunate results.

Thank you again for the feedback. Based on what you said, I’ve updated the post and added screenshots from the demo we worked on. Going forward, I’ll try to make better-quality posts based on this feedback and continue sharing our development process more clearly.

replies.author: alexpopescu801
replies.body: Thanks for replying. Yeah looks good to see the pictures in there. Wishing you the best with this project and other ones in the future

comments.author: rekansebangku
comments.body:
Interesting, whats your approach and method to tackle the living NPC ? Will the player use their own key? And how do you manage to maintain the NPC memory? 

I also interested in your 2d to 3d workflow, does this using API to generate?

replies.author: kkogong07
replies.body:
Thanks for your interest.

Right now, we’re developing the NPC system using Graphiti. Each NPC has five desires : **hunger, energy, loneliness, belonging, and curiosity** (I just have researched about this topic, and one paper suggest this approach), and their behavior is driven by those needs.

We also manage conversations between NPCs by turning them into a knowledge graph with Graphiti. Since Graphiti can handle data along a timeline as well, we’re currently researching how to make the best use of that for NPC memory.

For the 2D to 3D workflow, we don’t use an external API. We run Trellis.2 directly ourselves.

You can try it here:

[https://echo-town.com/](https://echo-town.com/)

A lot of creations have already been generated in just one day!
